newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Student riots force closure of Zambian university.
newsitem.headline: Student riots force closure of Zambian university.

text.p: The Zambian government on Monday ordered the closure of the country's biggest university after student riots in which 17 British Airways crew members were among those injured.

Police on Monday used teargas and batons to disperse students demonstrating against the blocking of a planned march to the presidential residence in opposition to plans for general elections scheduled for November 18.

A student leader was arrested and several others were slightly injured as police dispersed the demonstrators, who had planned to call on President Frederick Chiluba to reopen talks with the opposition, and possibly suspend the polls until all parties reached consensus on rules governing the elections.
"The University of Zambia has been closed with immediate effect following three days of student unrest on the campus," the university senate later said in a statement.
Riot police sealed off the university while transport was arranged to ferry students away from the Lusaka campus.
The riot was the second in three days on the university campus. On Saturday, 17 BA crew members were injured, some seriously, when students attacked their bus with stones.
Police said four BA staffers were subsequently flown to South Africa for specialist treatment.

Seven opposition parties, including former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP), are boycotting the polls which they claim have been arranged to ensure that Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD) remains in power.

The parties are opposed to a new constitution that bans some candidates, including Kaunda, from contesting the presidential race. They are also unhappy with the voters' register, which they say omits 2.3 million of the 4.6 million eligible voters.

Western governments, which share the opposition concerns, have cut or frozen aid to Zambia in an attempt to persuade the government to drop the contentious constitutional clauses and reopen the voters register.
The Chiluba government has dug in its heels and says it will not be dictated to by foreign governments.
